title: Study Abroad Report: Studying Abroad at Johns Hopkins University
paragraphs: 1. Until going to the United States 2. Clerkship in medical oncology 3. Clerkship in ophthalmology 4. Days off and daily life 5. Finally

1. Until going to the United States For two months, from April 20 to June 17, 2016, I was fortunate to have the opportunity to train in medical oncology and ophthalmology at Johns Hopkins University. Studying abroad had been a goal since I entered university, so I had no hesitation in applying. I chose America because I thought it would be difficult to learn medicine without understanding the language. I wavered over which university to choose because of safety and money, but pushed by my parents, and wanting to see the top class in America, I decided on Johns Hopkins University. Until going to America it was a series of hard things, beginning with studying for the TOEFL, then applying for the study abroad, submitting documents to the university and deciding the clerkship departments, and there were many documents even after I went. I had heard that sometimes the clerkship departments are not decided before the study abroad, but although I used connections and so on, they were decided without problems, which was a relief.

2. Clerkship in medical oncology Medical oncology is divided into three teams: Solid Tumor, Leukemia, and MLT (Myeloma, Lymphoma, Transplant). For the first two weeks I trained on the Solid Tumor team, and for the latter two weeks on MLT. The Solid Tumor team handled only patients with end-stage cancer, who were admitted when there was some complication. I was bewildered at first by having my patients die and by being present at critical moments many times. Everything I saw felt new: the very large number of Clinical Trials, outpatient visits having a 1.5-hour slot with plenty of time for rounds too, and the completely different degree to which patients and families engage with medical knowledge and treatment policy. I was told things like "Think about the second line for your patient and find papers that support it," and I grasped each day's patient trends and presented at the morning and evening conferences, and I was allowed to take charge of more than ten patients in just two weeks, which was very educational. In the latter two weeks, I followed patients on MLT undergoing hematopoietic stem cell transplantation. At Johns Hopkins University, hematopoietic stem cell transplantation is performed by HLA Haploidentical BMT, a method rare even in the world, and the leading doctors in that field were gathered there. As a result, I learned many experiences and stories that overturned my image of hematology in Japan; specifically, I was truly surprised that hematopoietic stem cell transplantation is done in the outpatient clinic, that patients are admitted if there are complications, and that even on the ward children, family, pets, flowers and so on can be brought in and patients live a life like ordinary patients. I had thought that these days it is determined by guidelines and the treatment seldom varies by country or place, but for hematopoietic stem cell transplantation it was different, and I had a valuable experience.

3. Clerkship in ophthalmology Ophthalmology is one of the popular departments in America too, and I chose and trained in it out of a wish to see it. Johns Hopkins has the Wilmer Eye Institute, the oldest ophthalmology facility in the country, and the residents here were all excellent people who passed a competition rate of 100 to 1. The main reasons for its popularity are apparently the high quality of life and pay and the thriving research, and in America the sense of being an elite is very strong, and I was surprised at the difference from Japan. In the clerkship, I was able to train while being stimulated by the local students, attending classes and surgical simulators with them and interviewing and examining patients in the outpatient clinic. In ophthalmology, African American patients who live near the hospital also came, and I was able to catch a glimpse of the gap with the wealthy who come from all over the country. While African Americans come to the hospital after going blind in one eye and about to go blind in both, or after having done so, there were also many wealthy people who flew in all the way from the West Coast every six months because they worried that they might have a cataract. Experiencing the fact that differences in wealth and the presence or absence of health insurance change the hurdle to seeing an ophthalmologist this much was also very educational.

4. Days off and daily life Baltimore cannot at all be said to be safe, but I was able to live more comfortably than I had imagined. It was hard because unless I spoke up and acted on my own, there were few chances to make local friends or friends among the exchange students, but it also became an opportunity to think that I must have that kind of proactiveness. Once I had made friends, it was not dangerous to go about in a large group, and above all I was able to have a very enjoyable life abroad. Washington D.C., New York and Philadelphia are also close, so I could meet friends and go sightseeing.

5. Finally Finally, I would like to thank very much the people of the International Collaboration Office who looked after me from the preparation stage for this study abroad, especially Dr. 長谷川 and 西尾-san. My parents, my friends, and 呉山-san, who was with me at SGUL, helped me on so many occasions from the preparation stage through the two months of study abroad, and I was able to finish the study abroad safely. This study abroad became a valuable opportunity to acquire knowledge that goes beyond medicine alone, to hear various opinions about my own future and the healthcare system, and to think for myself. I would like to make use of this experience and continue studying so that I can become the doctor I idealise.
